flashcards.q: What is a decision matrix?
flashcards.a: A grid that compares options on one page, scoring each against weighted criteria.
flashcards.more: First you agree the criteria (for example cost, security, time) and give each a weight. Then you score every option on each one. Score times weight, summed, gives the total. That moves the argument from "my favorite" to "which criterion matters more".

flashcards.q: Why must the criteria weights be fixed before scoring?
flashcards.a: Otherwise you're tempted to change the weights so your favorite wins, and the result is decided in advance.
flashcards.more: Arranging the criteria in favor of the option you like happens without you noticing. Writing the weights down and getting the team to agree first blocks that bias. If people disagree about a weight, that is the moment to discuss it.

flashcards.q: What is a sensitivity check, and why do it?
flashcards.a: Changing the weights to see if the winner changes. If it does, the decision hangs on an assumption about the weights.
flashcards.more: When the totals are close, a small change in weights can flip the result. That shows the real disagreement is not about the options but about which criterion matters more. Discussing that makes the decision stronger.

flashcards.q: Which decisions can be made quickly, and which slowly?
flashcards.a: Reversible ones (flag, library) quickly. Irreversible ones (public API, data model) slowly, and with discussion.
flashcards.more: When the cost of reversing is low, you can learn even from a mistake, so delay only wastes the chance. When reversing takes months, give yourself time to think and ask others. More in [[thinking/reversible-decisions/two-doors|reversible decisions]].

flashcards.q: Why write down your assumptions when deciding under uncertainty?
flashcards.a: When real data arrives, you can check it against them, see which one was wrong, and know when to revisit the decision.
flashcards.more: If the decision notes "we assume 2,000 messages a day", everyone knows it's time to rethink the moment the number is passed. If it isn't written down, the assumption lives in one person's head, and when they leave, the reason goes with them.

flashcards.q: How is a risk score calculated?
flashcards.a: Likelihood × impact, each scored 1 to 5. Handle the larger scores first.
flashcards.more: When likelihood is high but impact is small (an expert on leave), a cheap action is enough. When likelihood is low but impact is huge (payments down), it still needs attention. Taking both together makes the priority clear.

flashcards.q: What does it mean to "accept" a risk?
flashcards.a: To decide knowingly that you will do nothing about it, and to write that down.
flashcards.more: You can't remove every risk, and you don't need to. But quietly ignoring a risk is not the same as accepting it in writing. A written acceptance shows someone thought it through, and lets you look again if circumstances change.

flashcards.q: What is the sunk cost fallacy?
flashcards.a: Carrying on down the wrong path because you've already spent on it. The decision should rest only on future cost and benefit.
flashcards.more: Three months of effort won't come back, whether you carry on or throw it away. So the new question is: from here, what does it cost to finish, and what does the alternative cost? Pick the cheaper one. It feels hard because it means admitting your earlier decision was wrong.

flashcards.q: You've spent 12 weeks on a module. Finishing needs 4 more weeks; a standard replacement needs 1. What now?
flashcards.a: Switch. Compare only the future: 4 weeks against 1. The 12 weeks are gone either way. If the numbers were the other way around, you would finish.
flashcards.more: The rule is not "always drop what you built". It is "judge each path by what is still to be paid". Often that means switching, and sometimes it means finishing. Either way, write down the numbers you used.

flashcards.q: How should you explain the same design to four audiences?
flashcards.a: Start with each one's core question: how for the engineer, what changes for product, how much for finance, and proof for the auditor.
flashcards.more: You don't need four different decisions for four audiences; the design is the same. Only the order and the language change. Start with the answer to the listener's question, and they will listen to the rest.

flashcards.q: What three questions does a finance audience ask?
flashcards.a: How much will it cost? What do we get? What is the loss if we don't do it?
flashcards.more: Answer all three in one line, with numbers. If a number is an estimate, give a range (for example 6,000 to 10,000). Technical detail is beside the point for finance; a decision needs a comparison of cost and risk.

flashcards.q: What mistake is most common when explaining a design to a product manager?
flashcards.a: Hiding what is being given up in the user experience, or describing it in technology words.
flashcards.more: Say "the email will arrive 2 minutes late" and product can decide. Say "we'll use a queue" and they can't. If you hide the trade-off, it comes back later as a user complaint and a surprise.

flashcards.q: What does an auditor or regulator want?
flashcards.a: Proof: who did what and when, where the data lives, and how each control works.
flashcards.more: Saying "we work securely" isn't enough. You have to show the audit log, the access controls and a record of where the data sits. If you think about this at design time, you won't scramble during the audit.

flashcards.q: What does RFC stand for, and what is it for?
flashcards.a: Request for Comments: a 1-2 page document with the problem, options, proposal and risks, used to gather feedback and reach a decision.
flashcards.more: Spoken decisions get lost over time. With an RFC on file, even a new member six months later can see why a decision was made. Put the decider and the feedback deadline at the very top.

flashcards.q: Which option should an RFC always include?
flashcards.a: "Do nothing", so the reader can see whether the work is really worth its price.
flashcards.more: Many proposals show just one solution, which makes it look as if nothing else was considered. Show at least two options, including "do nothing", and the reader can compare for themselves.

flashcards.q: What is an ADR?
flashcards.a: Architecture Decision Record: a short note with a decision's context, the decision and its consequences, stored in the repo.
flashcards.more: An RFC is for a larger proposal; an ADR is the record kept once the decision is made. Each ADR is a few lines: what was decided, why, and what follows. Keeping it next to the code makes it easy to find.

flashcards.q: What harm comes when a design review turns into a courtroom?
flashcards.a: The author hides weaknesses out of fear, so the real risk is only caught in production.
flashcards.more: A question aimed at the person ("why didn't you think of this?") sends the author into self-defense. A question aimed at the design ("what if it breaks?") gets them to name the weak spot themselves. More in [[thinking/design-review/unstated-assumptions|design review]].

flashcards.q: What does influence without a title rest on?
flashcards.a: Trust: being regularly right, bringing numbers and evidence, and understanding other people's problems.
flashcards.more: A title can force people to follow orders, but it can't win their real agreement. Trust grows when you keep small promises, listen first and admit your own mistakes. That trust stays even when the title changes.

flashcards.q: What do you do first when you want the team to accept a proposal?
flashcards.a: Listen first: understand everyone's problems, then present your proposal as the answer to them.
flashcards.more: When you learn other people's problems before sharing your idea, the proposal becomes a way to make their own work easier. It turns from "your idea" into "our solution". It is the cheapest and most effective route.

flashcards.q: Why is a small pilot good for a big change?
flashcards.a: Low risk means permission comes easily, and with evidence in hand, the case for the big decision gets stronger.
flashcards.more: Ask permission for a refactor of the whole system and the answer is "no". Ask for a two-day trial in one module and the answer is "yes". A week later, show the result with numbers, and you won't need to persuade people again for the next step.

flashcards.q: Why ask questions instead of giving answers in mentoring?
flashcards.a: The junior works it out and can solve it alone next time. A direct answer fixes only today's problem.
flashcards.more: Questions such as "What have you tried?" and "What do you see in EXPLAIN?" teach a way of thinking. But if production is down, or the topic is completely new, help directly first and teach afterwards.

flashcards.q: Does consensus mean everyone agrees?
flashcards.a: No. It means there is no serious objection, and everyone is ready to move ahead with the decision.
flashcards.more: If you wait for everyone to agree completely, no decision ever happens. The question to ask is "Does anyone have a serious objection?" If not, you can move ahead even if nobody is fully on board, and you record the dissent.

flashcards.q: What is a pre-wire?
flashcards.a: Talking one on one, before the meeting, with the main objectors or the people the decision affects.
flashcards.more: When people hear an idea for the first time in a meeting, they say "no" to protect themselves. Talk privately first and they get time to think and raise objections, and there are no surprises in the meeting.

flashcards.q: What is "disagree and commit"?
flashcards.a: Working wholeheartedly for a decision even though you disagree with it. Your dissent is recorded beforehand.
flashcards.more: In discussion, you can state your disagreement openly, but once a decision is made, you can't work against it by the back door. If new facts come in, you can raise the question again. That way the team doesn't get stuck in arguments.

flashcards.q: When should you not use "disagree and commit"?
flashcards.a: When the decision is hard to undo, when the objection is about safety, security, law or ethics, or when new facts have arrived.
flashcards.more: The method cuts the cost of argument on decisions you can reverse. Deleting data or signing a contract with no exit needs evidence first. A safety, security or legal objection is not a dissent to log; it is a reason to stop and escalate.

flashcards.q: What do you need to stop an argument and decide?
flashcards.a: A deadline for the discussion, one decider, a record of dissent, and a condition for revisiting.
flashcards.more: With these four, the argument stays bounded, responsibility is clear, dissent is heard, and the decision isn't locked in forever. If you write them in a decision log, you can find the reason even six months later.

flashcards.q: What does it mean to turn a business goal into a design constraint?
flashcards.a: To convert business talk ("lots of customers on Black Friday") into a measurable quality with numbers ("500 orders/min").
flashcards.more: You can't design from words like "fast", "secure" or "a lot". Asking for numbers shows how much is needed and how much is spare. This translation is one of the architect's most important jobs.

flashcards.q: Which design decisions follow from "customers must never lose money"?
flashcards.a: Correctness and audit: transactions, a ledger, idempotency. Here, accuracy matters more than speed.
flashcards.more: There is no room to compromise with money. A double charge or a lost transaction damages trust. So you decide up front that this part gets the strictest rules. More in [[ledgers/modeling-money/float-trap|modeling money]].

flashcards.q: How is ROI calculated?
flashcards.a: ROI = (yearly gain − cost) ÷ cost. A cost of $30,000 and a gain of $60,000 is 100%.
flashcards.more: ROI shows what percentage comes back. Look at payback alongside it: how many months until the cost is earned back. With a cost of $30,000 and a yearly gain of $60,000, you gain $5,000 a month, so payback is 6 months.

flashcards.q: What are the limits of ROI?
flashcards.a: The gain figures are estimates, and value like security or risk reduction is hard to measure in money.
flashcards.more: Compliance and backup work looks small in ROI, yet skipping it can cost enormously. So look at ROI and the risk list together. When you quote numbers, give a range, such as "$40,000 to $60,000".

flashcards.q: When time is short, where can you cut corners?
flashcards.a: Where a mistake is cheap and easy to fix later, such as admin pages and rarely used reports. Never on money, security or data.
flashcards.more: Not all trade-offs are equal. You can give where customers don't directly notice and where it is easy to fix. When you do, write it down as a debt, set a date to repay it, and tell the business about the risk.

flashcards.q: What should you do when you take on debt to ship faster?
flashcards.a: Write it down, set a date to repay it, and tell the business.
flashcards.more: A hidden debt grows: nobody knows about it, so nobody repays it, and one day it turns up as a big problem. A written-down debt is a deliberate choice, not a regret. More in [[thinking/tech-debt/interest-grows|tech debt]].

flashcards.q: Why do you need to know legal rules at the start of design?
flashcards.a: Changing data location, retention and access later is expensive. Assume the rules up front and the design is right first time.
flashcards.more: Cloud region, database and log structure are settled early. Changing them later to follow a rule can take months. Don't interpret a specific law yourself; talk to compliance or a legal expert.

flashcards.q: What five questions turn legal rules into design?
flashcards.a: What data? Where will it live? For how long? Who can see it? What proof will you show an auditor?
flashcards.more: The five questions start from a list of your data. The answers decide where the database sits, how deletion works, how access is controlled and what the audit log holds. Write the answer to each one down.

flashcards.q: What can go wrong if you learn the legal rules only after launch?
flashcards.a: Data, backups and logs may have to move while live customers keep using the app, which can take months.
flashcards.more: Say a loan app keeps its data in a cloud region abroad, and a rule later says financial data must stay in the US. Now the database, backups, logs and analytics exports all have to move. One question in the first week avoids that bill.

flashcards.q: How does a rule like "delete rejected ID photos after 90 days" become part of the system?
flashcards.a: As a scheduled job that deletes the data and writes an audit_log row for each deletion, so you can prove it ran.
flashcards.more: The 90 days is written once, in the job's query. Delete and log happen in one statement, so a photo is never gone without a record. The 90 days and 7 years in this example are made up; the real figures come from compliance.

flashcards.q: What are the four kinds of teams in Team Topologies?
flashcards.a: Stream-aligned, Platform, Enabling and Complicated-subsystem.
flashcards.more: A stream-aligned team handles one flow of the business. A platform team provides tools to the others. An enabling team teaches new skills. A complicated-subsystem team looks after a hard specialist part. More in [[thinking/conways-law/three-team-queue|Conway's Law]].

flashcards.q: Why does cognitive load matter when splitting teams?
flashcards.a: A team can hold only so much in its head. Give it too much and both quality and speed suffer.
flashcards.more: Split teams so that each one fully understands its own area. If the hard specialist part or the tooling goes to a separate team, the stream team can focus on the business work.

flashcards.q: When should you not split engineers into the four team types?
flashcards.a: With fewer than about 10 engineers. One team can cover everything, and four labeled teams add hand-offs and no help.
flashcards.more: Split when you can see the pain: releases queue behind one person, a bug waits for its one expert, or nobody understands the whole system. Until then, a single small team talks faster than four.

flashcards.q: What is a "Now / Next / Later" roadmap?
flashcards.a: Three levels instead of exact dates: Now is committed, Next is likely, Later is uncertain.
flashcards.more: Far-off dates carry more uncertainty, and exact feature dates make false promises. With three levels, the business knows what it can rely on and what may change. Writing outcomes, not features, is a good habit too. If a law or a festival fixes a date, write that date down; the three levels are for work whose date is soft.

flashcards.q: What do you record for each dependency in a dependency register?
flashcards.a: The owner, the date we need it, the current status and the risk.
flashcards.more: Nobody watches a dependency with no owner. When the needed-by date is close and the status is behind, flag it red every week, so the delay is caught early and not at the last minute.

flashcards.q: What is the three-point estimate formula?
flashcards.a: Expected = (best + 4 × likely + worst) ÷ 6. This is known as PERT.
flashcards.more: For example, with best 3, likely 5 and worst 10, (3 + 20 + 10) ÷ 6 = 5.5 days. The most likely value gets four times the weight. The formula doesn't remove estimation error, but it does bring the bad case into the calculation.

flashcards.q: Instead of a single number, what do you give when asked for an estimate?
flashcards.a: A range and assumptions: "About 18 days, most likely 15 to 21, if the vendor sandbox arrives on time."
flashcards.more: People hear a single number as a promise. A range shows the uncertainty, and written assumptions make it easy to discuss the cause if they prove wrong. Shrink the biggest source of uncertainty first.

flashcards.q: How do you turn three-point estimates into a range for the whole job?
flashcards.a: Spread of a task = (worst − best) ÷ 6. Total spread = square root of the sum of the squares. Range = expected total ± that spread.
flashcards.more: Take tasks with spreads 1.2, 0.7 and 2.5: the squares add to about 8.2 and the root is 2.9. With an expected total of 18, the range is 15 to 21 days, about two chances in three. A shared risk, like one late vendor, sits outside this maths: write it as an assumption.

flashcards.q: Which two terms do you check in a vendor contract to avoid lock-in?
flashcards.a: The format and timing of getting your data back, and the exit terms (notice and penalty).
flashcards.more: If you can't get your data back, or leaving is expensive, you can't switch vendors, and you lose your bargaining power. Also check the SLA and its compensation, the price-rise terms and the liability cap. More in [[thinking/build-vs-buy/too-many-machines|build vs buy]].

flashcards.q: What does a 99.9% uptime promise (SLA) still allow?
flashcards.a: About 43 minutes of downtime a month. 99% allows over 7 hours. The promise is only worth the compensation behind it.
flashcards.more: A month has about 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is about 43. Ask what the vendor pays you when it misses the number, and how downtime is measured.

flashcards.q: Why use a hiring scorecard?
flashcards.a: To score every candidate on the same criteria with evidence, so the decision rests on skill, not on "I liked them".
flashcards.more: The criteria and weights are fixed first. Each interviewer writes their own scores and evidence separately, and only then do you discuss. That reduces one person's influence and exposes bias.

flashcards.q: What is resume-driven development?
flashcards.a: Choosing new technology to beef up your own CV, not because the project needs it.
flashcards.more: It adds complexity to the project, and the team has to handle it. Writing down the problem, the alternatives and the cost before choosing a technology helps you catch this tendency.

flashcards.q: What is the first question when evaluating new technology?
flashcards.a: Which of our problems does it solve, and do we really have that problem?
flashcards.more: Without a problem, a solution is extra cost however good it is. Show the problem in numbers: how slow, how many hours lost. After that come the questions about cost, alternatives and proof.

flashcards.q: What kind of proof is credible for new technology?
flashcards.a: Experience from someone our size who has run it in production for at least two years. Not the vendor's blog.
flashcards.more: Most problems with new technology appear months or years into production. So look for user experience, discussions of its limits and failure stories, and match them to your own size.

flashcards.q: What is a spike?
flashcards.a: A small, time-boxed experiment (say, one week) to see whether a technology works in our situation.
flashcards.more: Before a big decision, run the new technology on one low-risk piece of work. Use the result to decide whether to adopt, reject or test more. Spike code can be thrown away. More in [[hands-on/prototyping-profiling/two-weeks-wrong-thing|prototyping and profiling]].

flashcards.q: Tools vs fundamentals: how do you split your learning time?
flashcards.a: Most of it on fundamentals (transactions, concurrency, networks, trade-offs); tools as needed, when work requires them.
flashcards.more: Tools and frameworks change every few years, but fundamental ideas don't. Knowing the fundamentals makes new tools easier to learn, because you already recognize the problem behind them. 2 hours a week on fundamentals plus one spike a month is a good habit.

flashcards.q: What does pragmatism over purity mean?
flashcards.a: Follow a rule where its problem exists, and take the simple path where it doesn't, once you understand the rule's purpose.
flashcards.more: Behind every rule is a problem. If your project doesn't have it, the rule is extra weight. But don't compromise on money, security and data. When you break a rule, write down why.

flashcards.q: What does YAGNI mean?
flashcards.a: You Aren't Gonna Need It: don't build extra complexity today just because "we might need it later".
flashcards.more: Layers or features built for an imagined future need mostly never get used, but the weight stays. When the problem becomes real, adding the solution then is cheap, especially where you can reverse it.

flashcards.q: Why fix a review date and measures along with a decision?
flashcards.a: So that six months later you can check whether the assumptions held, on facts, not opinions.
flashcards.more: A decision's results arrive over time. If the review date and measures aren't fixed in advance, "we'll look later" never happens, and you can pick the numbers you like afterwards. With one owner, the responsibility stays clear too.

flashcards.q: A team of 5 with 2,000 users wants Kubernetes. What goes in the "Revisit if" line of the evaluation?
flashcards.a: A number that would make the problem real, such as peak load passing 200 requests a second or 3 teams blocking each other's deploys.
flashcards.more: A "no" is only today's answer. A trigger someone can watch turns it into a plan: while the number stays low, nobody reopens the debate; when it is crossed, the question comes back with evidence.
